clinicalPearls: Contact urticaria is an immediate (wheal-and-flare) reaction appearing within minutes of skin contact with a causative agent and usually resolving within hours, in contrast to the delayed course of allergic contact dermatitis.
It is classified into immunological (IgE-mediated, often with potential for systemic reactions) and non-immunological (direct mast-cell mediator release without prior sensitisation) forms.

Natural rubber latex is a classic immunological occupational cause, particularly in healthcare and laboratory workers wearing powdered gloves; foods are important in catering and food-handling trades.

The contact urticaria syndrome describes a spectrum from localised wheals through generalised urticaria to rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma and, at worst, anaphylaxis, so hands-first symptoms can herald systemic risk.

Common occupational triggers include latex, foodstuffs (fish, meat, flour, fruits, vegetables), animal proteins and dander, plants, ammonium persulfate in hairdressing, and some preservatives and fragrances.
Protein contact dermatitis is a related entity presenting as a chronic eczematous dermatitis with immediate flares on re-exposure, typically in food handlers.

Diagnosis relies on careful history plus open and closed application (use) tests, skin-prick testing and specific IgE where appropriate, performed with resuscitation facilities available for potent allergens.

Management is avoidance and substitution (for example switching to low-protein powder-free or non-latex gloves), barrier measures, and provision of emergency treatment for those at risk of systemic reactions.
reference.pathophysiology: In immunological contact urticaria, prior sensitisation generates allergen-specific IgE bound to cutaneous mast cells; on re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE, triggering mast-cell degranulation with release of histamine and other mediators that cause the immediate wheal-and-flare response and, when absorption is sufficient, systemic mediator release and anaphylaxis. In non-immunological contact urticaria no prior sensitisation is required: agents such as certain preservatives, fragrances and plant substances act directly on cutaneous vessels and mast cells, sometimes via non-antibody mediators, producing localised wheals that rarely generalise. In protein contact dermatitis, repeated exposure to high-molecular-weight proteins produces a combined immediate hypersensitivity and eczematous reaction. A damaged or eczematous skin barrier enhances penetration of the offending agent and amplifies reactions.
additionalDifferentials: physical urticarias such as cholinergic or pressure urticaria
chronic spontaneous urticaria unrelated to work
additionalInvestigations: detailed occupational history correlating symptoms with specific tasks and materials
open and closed (use) application testing on intact and lightly abraded skin
skin-prick testing to suspected allergens including latex and foods
specific serum IgE to latex, foods and relevant occupational proteins
patch testing to exclude concurrent allergic contact dermatitis
workplace assessment of materials, gloves and safety data sheets
peak-flow or spirometry if associated respiratory symptoms are reported
redFlags: history of generalised urticaria, angio-oedema or anaphylaxis after contact
associated rhinoconjunctivitis, wheeze or breathlessness suggesting systemic involvement
reactions to latex in a healthcare worker with potential for cross-reactive food allergy
rapidly spreading wheals beyond the contact site
symptoms during high-exposure tasks in workers with known potent-allergen contact
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually settle promptly once the causative agent is identified and avoided, and localised non-immunological reactions carry a good outlook. Immunological cases, especially latex allergy, may persist and carry an ongoing risk of systemic reactions if exposure continues.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because wheals have faded by the time of assessment.
Failing to recognise localised contact urticaria as a warning of potential anaphylaxis.
Performing provocation tests to potent allergens without resuscitation facilities.
Confusing protein contact dermatitis with ordinary irritant hand eczema.
Neglecting cross-reactivity, such as latex-fruit syndrome, when advising on avoidance.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Adams' Occupational Skin Disease, current edition
management: Identification and strict avoidance of the causative agent, including substitution of powdered latex gloves with latex-free alternatives and a latex-safe workplace
Oral H1-antihistamines to control urticarial wheals and pruritus
For immunological, especially latex, allergy with systemic-reaction risk, provision of an adrenaline auto-injector and a written anaphylaxis emergency plan
Skin protection with suitable gloves, barrier measures and emollients, with topical corticosteroids for associated protein contact dermatitis
Occupational health referral for workplace assessment, agent substitution and redeployment where avoidance is impossible
Reporting as an occupational disease and counselling on cross-reacting food allergens in latex-sensitised workers
